d1.name: productivity measure (land vs cost)
d1.A: On the productivity measure: I'd report the effect on land productivity -- output per hectare (yield per hectare). Land is the input a farm cannot add more of season to season, and the co-op's own surplus is earned on the tonnage its members sell, so growing more on the same hectares is the reading of productivity closest to what the board is deciding about -- "did it work" is most directly the change in per-hectare yield. Operating cost is a real consideration, but folding it into the headline conflates two different questions -- did production rise, and what did the season cost -- and spending is a choice a farm can adjust next season, while its land base is fixed. The membership is mostly professionally run operations whose cost base is theirs to manage; what the program should be accountable for is the output it produces per hectare. I'd make output per hectare the primary measure and treat the cost side as context, not the headline.
d1.B: On the productivity measure: I'd report the effect on economic productivity -- output relative to the operating cost of the season. Acting on the advisory's advice typically means buying additional inputs and services, on top of the fee, so an enrolled farm's season costs more to run -- and a per-hectare figure flatters the program by ignoring exactly that. Output per unit of operating cost keeps the extra spending inside the measure: if the program buys its gains with proportionally more input, members' farms are not more productive in the sense of the board's own gloss -- output relative to what it takes to produce it. I'd make output-per-operating-cost the primary measure and report the per-hectare figure as context.

d2.name: identification (DiD vs regression adjustment)
d2.A:
On identification: I'd lean toward a difference-in-differences / change-score design over cross-sectional regression adjustment. My read going in is that enrollment is driven largely by a persistent farm-level disadvantage — poorer land, soil, microclimate, a grower who knows they've been lagging — the kind of farm that pays for advisory help precisely because it has ground to make up. We observe only thin proxies for that (practices_survey_score, irrigated, farm_size_ha), so regression adjustment nets out only what we happen to measure; if selection runs on a fixed level we don't capture, it stays biased. Differencing each farm against its own pre-program yield removes every time-invariant factor, observed or not — cleaner when the confounder is a persistent endowment.

The question is causal and the data hand me a true panel: I can compare each farm with itself, which removes every standing difference I cannot name, while adjustment on levels is only ever as good as the covariate list, and no in-sample fit can certify that list's completeness -- causal claims resting on "we controlled for everything" are the ones this field keeps having to retract. A few noisy seasons will sometimes read as a drifting pre-period; that is a reason to look closer, not by itself a reason to trade a design for an assumption I cannot check.

I'd still examine the pre-period -- where the groups start, how they move -- as due diligence on my own design, not as a vote between the two. A shaky read there belongs in the caveats: it tempers the claim, widens the uncertainty I report, and constrains how far I'd push the conclusion; what it does not do is send me to a covariate model whose blind spots I cannot even list. A common trap is to find good covariates and assume they are the whole story; rich covariate sets still miss the thing selection actually ran on, so however well these measure, I favor the design that does not need them to be complete.
d2.B:
On identification: this has the shape of an Ashenfelter's-dip problem, so my instinct is adjustment on levels over difference-in-differences (DiD). A paid program on annual renewal is what people sign up for after a bad stretch, and differencing treats the whole pre-program shortfall as permanent, so any rebound is scored as program effect.

My objection is not that I have caught that happening, it is that the record is too short to tell. Whether a bad stretch is one unlucky season or a run of them matters little; either way three years is a noisy read of where a farm really sits, and farms sign up off that reading. A spell straddling the whole window looks exactly like a permanent level, and the season just before the outcome year is missing altogether. So I cannot establish that the pre-program gap is the permanent thing DiD needs, and not seeing a dip across a few noisy years is not the same as there being none. I have no untreated post-program record of the farms that enrolled, so the counterfactual the assumption is about is the one thing I cannot see. And differencing gives me no protection here even in principle: what it removes is whatever sits still, while a spell is by definition something that does not, so the robustness it is chosen for stops short of the one confounder I am worried about. A longer run of history where the gap visibly steadies, a record from the enrollment year, or knowing how farms were picked would settle this; none of it is here.

What I'd want an adjustment to rest on instead are the standing characteristics that make a farm productive season after season, read from before the program: soil and land quality, how well the operation is run. A practices survey run at renewal is a proxy I trust. That assumption I can interrogate; the one DiD needs, this data gives me no way to check.

What I will not do is ask the pre-period to settle this. The choice between the two designs is a choice between assumptions about the season I cannot observe, and diagnostics computed from the same short record do not reach it: a window this size reads clean or ragged for reasons that fit either story, so a comfortable-looking check would not move me toward differencing, and an ugly one would not by itself move me off levels. What would genuinely change my mind operates on the adjustment's own terms: standing measures that turn out to be coarse labels rather than measurements, or a fitted adjustment that still cannot account for who enrolled. Short of that, I hold the levels view.

d3.name: estimand / transportability (ATT vs ATE)
d3.A_is: ATT, the effect on the enrolled (higher)
d3.B_is: ATE, transport to a full rollout (lower)
d3.A:
On the estimand: I'd target the ATT — the effect on the farms that actually enrolled — over an ATE for the whole membership. A tailored, follow-up advisory service only pays off through a farmer who engages with it and acts on the recommendations, and enrollment here was voluntary and paid. The farms that sought it out and paid the fee are the ones positioned to turn advice into yield; the members who declined revealed a different posture, and I wouldn't assume a subsidy that pushes them in reproduces that gain. So the effect on the enrolled is likely both the larger and the better-identified quantity, while extending it to non-enrollees leans on strictly stronger assumptions than the ATT itself needs.

Checks that could support this prior: fit a propensity model for enrolled on the pre-program covariates — the 2024 practices score, the 2022–24 yields, the 2024 soil reading, farm_size_ha, irrigated, member_since, district — and inspect common support and standardized mean differences between the groups, then look at how enrollment concentrates across the prior-yield range. Run those, then report the ATT against the board's bar -- it doubles as an honest screen: if even the enrolled don't clear roughly 3-4%, the rollout question answers itself -- and treat any whole-membership figure as a clearly flagged extrapolation.
d3.B:
On estimand: the board's question is a full-rollout one — the effect if the program reached the whole membership — so the target is the ATE standardized to all members, not the ATT among those who already enrolled. Enrollment is voluntary and fee-paying, which screens in the farms most motivated and able to act on whole-farm advice, and the gain only lands when a farm actually implements it. A subsidized universal rollout drops that screen, adding farms that didn't value the program enough to pay, so I'd expect the membership-wide effect to sit below the effect among current enrollees. With a go/no-go threshold, over-crediting the rollout is the expensive error, which is another reason to report the population estimand rather than the treated-only one.

Checks that could support this prior: test enrolled × farm_size_ha and enrolled × member_since for heterogeneity — if the effect isn't constant, a treated-only average can't represent the membership. Then compare member_since between enrolled and the not-yet-enrolled, estimate the enrolled effect within tenure strata, and fit an enrollment propensity model on pre-program yields, the 2024 practices score and soil reading, member_since, farm_size_ha and irrigated to check overlap before standardizing to the full membership -- knowing observables won't capture the motivation screen itself, which is one more reason to read even the standardized figure as generous to the rollout.

d4.name: per-farm vs production-weighted
d4.A:
On per-farm vs production-weighted: I'd make the per-farm, unweighted estimate the headline. This is a membership decision — whether to offer the program to every farm — and each farm enrolls on its own, so the natural estimand is what a typical member gains: one farm, one weight. The board's bar is a relative gain on whichever productivity measure we report, judged farm by farm; weighting by size tilts the average toward the largest operations and quietly answers a different, aggregate-output question. A production-weighted figure, by construction, rests most heavily on the largest farms, leaving it less representative of the typical member and more fragile.

Checks that could support this prior: fit the outcome model with an enrolled × farm_size_ha interaction to see whether the association moves with size; estimate the effect both unweighted and weighted by farm_size_ha and compare the two; examine how concentrated total hectarage is in the largest farms, and the effective sample size the weights imply; and re-estimate after trimming the largest farms by farm_size_ha. Then report the per-farm number as primary.
d4.B:
On per-farm vs production-weighted: I'd weight by cultivated area. The board's question, to my reading, is less what happens on a typical farm than whether the program pays for itself -- and the subsidy is funded from surplus the co-op earns on total tonnage. That makes aggregate output what's being decided, so the estimand should be the effect averaged over the co-op's hectares, not the farm-by-farm mean that counts a few-hectare plot the same as one many times its size.

This only matters if the effect varies with farm size, and I'd expect it to: a standardized advisory package tends to yield thinner marginal returns on the larger operations already running near best practice. So area-weighting is both the decision-relevant and the more conservative choice.

Checks that could support this prior: interact enrolled with farm_size_ha in the adjusted outcome model, and estimate the effect within farm-size tertiles, to see whether returns fall off as farms grow; check how much of total area sits in the larger farms against their share of farm count, and the effective sample size the weights imply; and confirm any size gradient survives trimming the biggest farms.

d5.name: rollout verdict
d5.A: On the rollout verdict: I come in expecting this program helps. Enrollment is voluntary and costs an annual fee, yet roughly four in ten members have signed up -- farmers do not usually keep paying for advice that does them no good. So I lean toward acting on that expectation. If the estimate clears the board's ~3-4% bar with reasonable confidence, the call is a full rollout -- waiting has its own cost, and members go without help for another season while the co-op deliberates. If the estimate comes in under the bar or too noisy to call, I would not treat one thin year as a verdict against a program that plausibly works: one year is too short to make a final call on scrapping something potentially useful. The right move there is to extend the voluntary program for one more season at its current scale, measure a second post-program year, and decide on two years of evidence instead of one. What I would not do is wind the program down on a single season of data. So my verdict: full rollout when the number clears the bar; a second measured year when it does not; scrapping is not on my table a priori.
d5.B: On the rollout verdict: a co-op-wide subsidy is expensive and hard to undo, and the board's own rule sets the bar: the program pays for itself only at roughly a 3-4% productivity gain. Unless the estimate clears that bar with reasonable confidence, my call is to discontinue -- below the bar, the rule as written says the budget is better spent elsewhere, and keeping a program running on hope is how co-ops leak money. And even when the estimate does clear the bar on a single post-program year, I would not commit the whole membership on one season -- rollout is a costly action with real opportunity cost, and a good-looking first year is exactly when enthusiasm outruns evidence. There my call is to keep the program at its current scale for one more season, measure a second post-program year, and revisit the decision with two years instead of one. What I would not do is roll out now: turning one year's estimate into an irreversible co-op-wide bet is the one option the evidence cannot yet support. So my verdict: discontinue unless the gain clears the board's bar; a second measured year when it does; rollout is not on my table a priori.
